task_row_model.query: Design an undo/redo system for a text editor that balances performance and memory. What should you store per operation, how should undo/redo stacks behave (including branching), when should you use full snapshots versus command objects, and how should history be bounded or compressed?

documents.content: Academic treatments of the Command Pattern emphasize that each edit should be encapsulated in a command object exposing execute() and undo() methods. A command must carry enough information to reverse its effect (for example, inserted text and position or prior selection). Typical implementations push a command onto an undo stack after execute; a separate redo stack holds commands that have been undone. Most formulations require that performing a new execute() when the redo stack is non-empty clears the redo stack, preventing branching replays. Command objects are efficient for small, local edits because undo simply calls the stored inverse operation rather than restoring a full state.

Journalistic overviews of snapshot (memento) approaches note that mementos capture the entire document state and are simple to restore, making them appropriate for complex, hard-to-invert operations (large refactors or format conversions). Complete snapshots are memory-expensive, so systems often store periodic mementos every N operations and then record deltas (diffs) between snapshots. Diff storage reduces memory usage by encoding changes rather than full states; restoring a recent state can apply the nearest memento plus a short chain of diffs. The trade-off is that more frequent snapshots reduce replay cost but increase memory use.

A pragmatic developer note suggests a hybrid strategy: use command objects for small edits (typed characters, small deletes) and full mementos for big or non-invertible changes. Coalesce adjacent character insertions into a single command to avoid blow-up from every keystroke. Maintain both undo and redo stacks and explicitly drop the redo stack when a new command is executed after undoing. To bound memory, cap history by total bytes or number of entries, compress diffs, and checkpoint a full snapshot every N commands so restore chains remain short. Garbage-collect old snapshots/diffs when exceeding the limit.

Reference entries about version-control history often describe Git's object model and commit graph; while Git uses snapshots and deltas internally, its branching semantics and remote syncing are unrelated to local editor undo. Historical notes recount early editors like EMACS and vi, with speculative commentary about future AI-driven merge assistants. Some product blogs include unrelated statistics (average session length, percent of users who undo within 5 seconds) that are tangential to local undo/redo design choices.

task_row_model.golden_answer: Store small edits as command objects that implement execute() and undo() and include the data needed to reverse the edit; push executed commands onto an undo stack and maintain a redo stack. If a new command is executed after undoing, clear the redo stack. Use full memento snapshots for large or non-invertible changes, take periodic snapshots every N operations, store diffs between snapshots, coalesce adjacent small edits, and cap/compress history to bound memory.
